This story isn't about *all* the locations where solar can be installed - they're already rolling it out in agricultural fields where I live. The story is about a specific situation - using space that is otherwise unused to solve at least two problems (generating power + preventing water loss), while assessing any new problems (maintenance and cost, etc) that may emerge with the solution. 

To me, those structures look a little over-engineered - yes, panels have weight and need to be properly secured - but perhaps they're looking at the kind of inputs that will inform the structure design in specific situations/locations. 

The concerns some people had re narrower canals didn't make sense to me either - build narrower structures. Solar panels are modular units, after all, and can be assembled in all kinds of shapes. If access is too difficult, fine, don't build there. There will also be a formula needed to calculate if too many "gaps" in your deployment make it too inefficient, but for a long array, I doubt there will be a single exit point for exporting the electricity. Probably needs a formula to figure out if a section is "long enough" for the conditions and can be readily connected for export.

I'd personally support a new model of land use that would allow some development of 'almost' green belt regions, but in a combined model that retains sufficient land and space to be valid agricultural zone while also supporting office or industrial space.

This was the model used for the original San Jose IBM campus, a huge, sprawling, functional prune orchard with large industrial campus scattered within/throughout it. That was originally done for tax purposes, but it made for genuine sustainable use of land ... right up until tax breaks and subsidies were too limited (or dried up completely) to keep it economical for IBM, the orchard was allowed to go fallow (some trees survived unwatered, others died), then sold off to another company for office space, then sold off to a developer who sub-divided it (as the City changed the zoning), and it ended up completely paved over with parking lots and store fronts ... excessively large parking lots and store fronts that COULD hypothetically have been built with revitalizing the orchard in mind, or at least park-like open space with wildlife in mind (there was a LOT of wildlife there before it was all paved over, including multiple fields of fallow land that hadn't been used for the orchards for decades prior to the closure, either). A few apartment blocks were also built, but a satellite view will clearly show that those could have been built without destroying the land, so it was mostly the store fronts. (there's also controversy over arson that destroyed the oldest IBM building with historical significance that had been slated as a museum ... the fire led to that land being opened up for development)


So I would be in favor of more development similar to the best use cases from the 1960s with a modern spin on such (not just the green belt standard of no electricification, no plumbing, no gas, etc), while I am obviously in favor of maintaining existing industrial parks and the like that do maintain open space and green and potentially can support agricultural operation as well.


We did avoid the local disaster that the Coyote Valley Specific Plan would have been, far, far worse than what happened to IBM. (a massive sprawling development that would've paved over many farm plots, wildlands, and a seasonal lake ... and intended to force tens of thousands of residents into the region, and also dig out a major intersection to build an artificial lake in the middle of it, it all made no sense)

 The single power plant built was the only part of that project to go anywhere, and that was tainted by the Enron/Gray Davis energy scandal from 2002, but it at least adopted a reasonable industrial park type configuration within a local fallow field and is a modern, high efficiency, combined cycle natural gas power station (one that hypothetically could be converted to hydrogen power if/when enough large nuclear plants and surplus renewable power can pipeline hydrogen to it, or potentially take the other option: do CO2 capture and pipeline that to synthetic fuel plants adjacent to hydrogen production sites to turn the CO2 into syngas:  CO2 is MUCH more efficient to pipeline than hydrogen, and switching NG pipes to hydrogen has a lot of problems in materials and safety plus actual energy flow rate, so that might be a more realistic option long-term given that station is likely good for many more decades of operation;  synthetic methane would be a viable NG alternative, as would be dimethyl ether which is really efficient to make from syngas and close enough to methane and ethane combustion to be simple to convert the existing NG turbines to  .... this is all assuming that chemical battery storage doesn't vastly exceed the practical use of chemical energy storage/use in combustion fuels within the next 10-20 years;  using DME also makes more sense than a methanol pipeline given the physical and chemical properties and the compatibility of DME with existing NG pipelines as well as anything intended for LPG ...  but methane is also a low-value byproduct from a lot of synthetic fuel and chemical processes, so synthetic natural gas would still be a realistic possibility to consider, or a blend of methane and DME  ... ethane would likely be too valuable as ethylene feedstock to use as fuel)

Already on agrivoltaic farms livestock are grazing on pasture growing under elevated ground mounted solar arrays.  Plants benefit from the shade of the array and are shielded from heavy rains, hail and sun stress.  
Plants do have a limit on the amount of sunshine they can metabolize known as light saturation point.  Once a plant reaches this maximum rate of photosynthesis the plant starts evaporating water to cool itself.  Agrivoltaics reduce the amount of water evaporation from plants reducing water loss and agricultural water usage.

So, the next problem...
The Osage Nation seem to have sold the surface rights quite some time ago... but they retained the mineral rights.
This means that the wind farm company didn't need permission from the Osage to build the wind farm... at least on the surface of things.  (Pardon the pun!)  Nor did the Osage get paid... the owners of the SURFACE rights did.
